title: Prediction of high-risk factor in early-stage lung cancer: micropapillary adenocarcinoma

paragraphs.en: Micropapillary lung adenocarcinoma (MPA) is an aggressive histological subtype of invasive lung adenocarcinoma (LADC), characterized by a high propensity for lymphovascular invasion, distant dissemination, and early metastasis. Compared to well-differentiated (lepidic) and moderately differentiated (papillary or acinar) subtypes, MPA is associated with significantly poorer prognosis and increased recurrence risk even in early-stage disease [1]. Although MPA accounts for a relatively small proportion of LADCs, numerous studies have demonstrated that the presence of an MPA component is independently associated with worse clinical outcomes [2–4]. A study has found that MPA is a significant predictor of postoperative brain metastasis in patients with resected lung adenocarcinoma [5]. Even among patients with stage I lung adenocarcinoma, the 5-year overall survival rate for patients with MPA present ranges from 54% to 79%, compared to 73% to 98% in those without MPA involvement [6–13]. These findings underscore the clinical importance of accurate identification of MPA, particularly in early-stage disease, to optimize surgical and adjuvant management strategies.

Histopathological examination of tissue specimens remains the gold standard for subtype classification in LADC. However, the sensitivity of intraoperative frozen section analysis for detecting MPA is limited to approximately 37%, primarily due to inconsistencies between frozen and formalin-fixed paraffin-embedded (FFPE) sections [14]. Therefore, reliable preoperative prediction of MPA presence holds significant clinical value, as it enables more precise pathological classification and supports individualized treatment planning.

With the rapid advancement in radiomics and artificial intelligence, several studies have explored their potential in predicting histologic subtypes and aggressiveness of lung adenocarcinomas [15,16]. Although radiomics-based models integrating CT-derived features such as nodule density, margin characteristics, and internal heterogeneity have shown promise in identifying high-grade components, including MPA, there remains a lack of simple, interpretable, and clinically applicable predictive models specifically tailored for MPA. In this study, we retrospectively analyzed patients with stage IA–IB LADC to identify independent risk factors associated with MPA. Based on these findings, we established a predictive model and a corresponding nomogram to facilitate preoperative recognition of MPA. The ultimate goal is to enhance diagnostic precision, guide individualized surgical decision-making, and improve the overall prognosis of patients with early-stage LADC.

This study was approved by the Biomedical Ethics Committee of West China Hospital, Sichuan University. Patients who were pathologically diagnosed with LUAD at West China Hospital between January 2011 and June 2022 were included. To address the classification of patients, two experienced pathologists, each with over 10 years of diagnostic experience, independently reviewed all pathological slides. Based on the presence or absence of a micropapillary component (Supplementary Figure 1) in the tumor sections, patients were divided into the MPA group and the non-MPA group. In cases of disagreement, a senior pathologist with greater experience participated in the review, and the final classification was determined by consensus among the three pathologists. As solid adenocarcinoma is also considered a poorly differentiated, high-grade subtype of adenocarcinoma, cases with a solid component were excluded. Consequently, the pathological subtypes of patients in the non-MPA group included any combination of lepidic, acinar, and papillary patterns. Exclusion criteria were as follows: (1) Pathological stage II-IV disease; (2) Presence of other concurrent malignancies; (3) No surgical specimens; (4) Presence of other poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma components (e.g. solid, mucinous); (5) Diagnosis of multiple primary lung cancers; and (6) Incomplete or missing key clinical data.

Due to the significant disparity in patient numbers between the MPA and non-MPA groups, age and gender matching was conducted to establish a more consistent baseline across both groups. This matching procedure aimed to achieve an equal ratio of patients in the MPA group to those in the non-MPA group, set at 1:1. Clinical characteristics, pathological information, imaging data, treatment, and prognosis of patients in the two groups were collected and analyzed, respectively.

High-resolution chest computed tomography (HRCT) scans were reviewed for 680 patients using standard lung window settings (window width: 1800 HU; window level: −400 HU). Tumor location was described in terms of lung lobes (right upper lobe, right middle lobe, right lower lobe, left upper lobe, left lower lobe). The relevant imaging features were defined as follows (Two pulmonologists independently evaluated the imaging features. If their interpretations differed, a third pulmonologist reviewed the scans to reach a final consensus.):
Tumor size: the longitudinal diameter of the tumor cross-section at its maximum in all CT levels.

Density: solid nodule (SN) refers to a pulmonary nodule that is dense enough to cover the bronchial and vascular shadows; ground-glass opacity (GGO) refers to a lesion that is well or poorly demarcated but where the density of the lesion is not sufficient to cover the vasculature and bronchioles; partially-solid nodule (PSN): is a lesion containing both ground-glass and solid components within the same nodule; non-ground-glass nodule (non-GGO): refers to SN and PSN.
Lobulation: the presence of multiple convex or scalloped indentations along the tumor margin (Figure 1(A), red arrows)
Spiculation: tumor margins with varying degrees of spiny or burr-like projections (Figure 1(B), red arrows)
Vacuoles: single or multiple small punctate hypodense shadows within the tumor, not contiguous with the bronchioles (Figure 1(C), red arrows)
Pleural retraction: pleura retracted towards the tumor (Figure 1(C), white arrow)

Volume Doubling Time (VDT): the period it takes for the tumor volume to double (measured in days). The measurement follows a protocol outlined in a study published in the Journal of Thoracic Oncology [17]. Tumor volume was computed utilizing the formula V = (π/6) * a * b2, where a represents the maximum tumor diameter (Figure 1(D)) and b denotes the maximum vertical tumor diameter on the same plane (Figure 1(D)). VDT was determined using the formula VDT = (t * log2)/log (Vt/V0), where “t” stands for the interval between the two scans, “V0” is the tumor volume at the initial CT scan, and “Vt” represents the tumor volume at the preoperative CT scan. For the calculation of VDT, we required that the interval between the two follow-up scans exceeded two weeks, and missing VDT values were addressed using multiple imputation.

In this study, all procedures for data cleaning, statistical analysis, model construction, and visualization were conducted using R (version 4.4.1) and SPSS (version 25.0). Inter-observer consistency between the two pulmonologists was evaluated using the Intraclass Correlation Coefficient (ICC) for continuous measures and Cohen’s kappa for categorical imaging features. Continuous variables with normal distribution were presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD), while those with non-normal distribution were expressed as median with interquartile range (IQR). Comparisons between MPA and non-MPA groups were made using t-test for continuous variables and chi-square test for categorical variables. Univariate and multivariate logistic regression analyses were performed to identify variables significantly associated with the presence of MPA and to determine independent predictors. A logistic regression-based predictive model was constructed, and a nomogram was developed. ROC curves were applied to assess the optimal cutoff value for continuous variables predicting MPA and to evaluate the diagnostic performance of the predictive model. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

sections.title: Basic information in the MPA and non-MPA groups

paragraphs.en: According to our inclusion and exclusion criteria, a total of 340 patients with MPA were enrolled. Using 1:1 random matching, 340 non-MPA patients were selected as controls, yielding a final cohort of 680 individuals. The clinical, radiological, and pathological characteristics of patients in the training cohort are detailed below.

The proportion of smokers was significantly higher in the MPA group (31.2%) compared to the non-MPA group (22.6%) (p = 0.015). In both groups, tumors were more frequently located in the upper lobes of the lungs. In terms of prognosis, tumor recurrence occurred in 69 patients (23.2%) in the MPA group, significantly higher than in the non-MPA group, where only 6 patients (2.0%) experienced recurrence (p < 0.001). As shown in Table 1, the most common recurrence sites in the MPA group were intrapulmonary (33.3%), bone (24.6%), and brain (21.7%). In contrast, lymph node metastasis was more frequently observed in the non-MPA group (50.0%). Since only 191 MPA patients had clearly documented proportions, we stratified patients into two groups based on MPA proportion: those with MPA ≥20% and those with MPA <20%. Our analysis showed no significant difference in prognosis between the two groups (p = 0.552)

Pathological features also differed significantly between the two groups (Table 1). Tumors in the MPA group were significantly larger in diameter compared to those in the non-MPA group (p < 0.001). Additionally, the presence of spread through air spaces (STAS), vascular invasion, and pleural involvement were all more common in the MPA group (all p < 0.001). The most frequent histological subtypes in the MPA group were acinar predominant and papillary predominant, while in the non-MPA group, acinar predominant and lepidic predominant subtypes were more prevalent.

In terms of imaging characteristics (Table 1), the MPA group showed a significantly higher proportion of solid nodules, lobulation, spiculation, and pleural retraction compared to the non-MPA group (all p < 0.001), with good inter-observer consistency in evaluating these subjective CT features according to Cohen’s kappa (Supplementary Table 1). Furthermore, the volume doubling time (VDT) was significantly shorter in the MPA group, indicating more rapid tumor growth. As shown in Supplementary Table 2, the inter-observer consistency for VDT assessment was good, with ICC values demonstrating high consistency between readers.

sections.title: MPA as an independent predictor of prognosis in stage I lung adenocarcinoma

paragraphs.en: To further delineate factors associated with recurrence, we performed a univariable analysis incorporating sex, age, smoking status, family history of cancer, surgical resection type, pathohistological characteristics (including tumor diameter, STAS, vascular invasion, and pleural invasion), as well as key radiologic features. Univariable results indicated that lobectomy, pathohistological diameter, STAS, thrombosis of a vascular system, pleural invasion, the MPA component, pathological stage (IA3 and IB), CT-derived diameter, SN, lobulation, spiculation, and pleural retraction were significantly associated with worse prognosis (Supplementary Table 3). Furthermore, multivariable Cox regression analysis demonstrated that MPA was an independent risk factor associated with poorer prognosis (Table 2).

In addition, we examined the impact of different treatment strategies on the prognosis of patients in the MPA group. Given the limited number of patients who received targeted therapy in stage I or adjuvant chemotherapy in stage IA, we focused on evaluating the effect of surgical approach (lobectomy vs sublobar resection) on outcomes in all MPA patients and the effect of chemotherapy on outcomes in stage IB MPA patients. Although neither lobectomy versus sublobar resection nor chemotherapy versus no chemotherapy showed statistically significant differences in survival, the Kaplan–Meier curves suggested that long-term outcomes after lobectomy tended to be inferior to those after sublobar resection. Similarly, among patients with stage IB MPA, chemotherapy did not yield a significant overall survival advantage; however, a trend toward improved long-term prognosis was observed in the chemotherapy group compared with non-chemotherapy patients (Figure 2).

sections.title: Development and validation of a non-invasive MPA prediction model
Identification of risk factors associated with MPA

paragraphs.en: Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis was first performed to determine optimal cutoff values for continuous variables such as CT-diameter and VDT. Based on these thresholds, univariate logistic regression analysis was conducted. The analysis revealed that smoking, maximal diameter on CT ≥ 22.5 mm, PSN, SN, lobulation, spiculation, vacuole, pleural retraction, and VDT ≤ 310 days were all significantly positively correlated with MPA, with Odds Ratios (ORs) of 1.547 (95% CI [1.100, 2.183]), 5.147 (95% CI [3.660, 7.312]), 5.429 (95% CI [3.149, 9.796]), 54.690 (95% CI [31.243, 100.839]), 21.271 (95% CI [9.962, 55.229]), 13.300 (95% CI [8.014, 23.432]), 2.478 (95% CI [1.820, 3.387]), 3.805 (95% CI [2.686, 5.446]), and 6.596 (95% CI [4.720, 9.299]), respectively. Variance inflation factor (VIF) analysis revealed negligible multicollinearity among the included risk factors (Supplementary Table 4), and therefore all variables were retained for multivariable modelling. Multivariate logistic regression analysis based on the significant variables from the univariate analysis identified the following as independent risk factors for MPA: smoking, CT diameter ≥22.5 mm, PSN, SN, lobulation, spiculation, vacuole, and VDT ≤310 days (Table 3).

sections.title: Construction and validation of a non-invasive MPA prediction model and nomogram

paragraphs.en: A non-invasive prediction model for MPA was developed based on multivariate logistic regression analysis, with the following formula:
where “p” represents the predicted probability that the tumor contains a micropapillary component.

To facilitate clinical application, we presented a nomogram to estimate the individualized probability of MPA (Figure 3(A)). Besides, we have developed an online risk calculator to facilitate rapid preoperative estimation of MPA, which integrates the predictors from our nomogram into an interactive web-based tool. The calculator is publicly accessible at: https://mpariskassessment.shinyapps.io/MPA-risk-prediction/. Each predictor – including smoking, CT-diameter, density, lobulation, spiculation, vacuoles and VDT – is assigned a specific number of points according to its relative contribution in the multivariable logistic regression model. By summing the points for all variables, a total score is obtained, which corresponds to the predicted probability of MPA on the bottom scale. Higher total scores indicate a greater likelihood of MPA. To assess the calibration of the nomogram, we constructed a bootstrap-corrected calibration curve based on 1,000 resamples. As shown in Figure 3(B), the bias-corrected curve closely overlapped with the ideal reference line across the entire range of predicted probabilities. Furthermore, to evaluate its discriminative capacity, we generated a ROC curve for the nomogram. The model exhibited good discriminatory performance, with an AUC of 0.923(95%CI [0.903,0.944]) (Figure 3(C)). Additionally, in the Hosmer–Lemeshow test, the p-value was 0.1575, indicating good calibration with consistent agreement between the predicted and observed outcomes across risk groups (Supplementary Figure 2). Moreover, decision curve analysis (DCA) further demonstrated that the nomogram provided a higher net clinical benefit across a wide range of threshold probabilities compared with the treat-all and treat-none strategies, supporting its potential clinical utility (Figure 3(D)). In addition, using the Youden index, we selected 48.13% as the optimal cutoff probability for identifying MPA. The corresponding sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, negative predictive value, and F1-score were 87.35%, 86.18%, 86.34%, 87.20%, and 86.84%, respectively. Finally, we evaluated the consistency of the model across different subgroups (Figure 3(E)). Specifically, the AUCs for predicting MPA in patients with CT-diameter ≤2 cm, >2 cm, smokers, and non-smokers were 0.899, 0.906, 0.928, and 0.917, respectively, indicating stable predictive performance across these subpopulations. Meanwhile, we found that after stratifying patients in our cohort, 39.06% of high-risk patients experienced recurrence within 2 years, whereas all recurrences in the low-risk group occurred more than 2 years after surgery (p = 0.023). No significant differences were observed between high- and low-risk groups in terms of intrathoracic or distant recurrence (p = 0.152); however, high-risk patients were more likely to develop recurrence involving more than two distant sites. To further evaluate the potential role of nomogram-based risk stratification in guiding treatment decisions, we analyzed the impact of different treatment modalities on prognosis across different risk groups. Although no statistically significant differences were observed among the groups, a trend was noted in the high-risk group, in which patients who underwent lobectomy exhibited inferior long-term outcomes compared with those who received sublobar resection (Supplementary Figure 3).

In this study, we systematically compared the clinical and radiologic characteristics of patients with and without MPA and conducted Cox regression analysis to identify prognostic risk factors. The results revealed that MPA was an independent risk factor for poor prognosis in stage I lung adenocarcinoma, consistent with findings from previous studies [18,19]. Furthermore, we investigated the impact of different treatment on the prognosis of patients with MPA. We found that lobectomy or sublobar resection had no significant effect on the prognosis of patients with stage I MPA; even in long-term follow-up, the prognosis of lobectomy was inferior to that of sublobar resection. This is consistent with the previous research findings by Mathey-Andrews C. et al. [20]. Additionally, a multicenter study in Japan revealed that the reduction in lung function after segmentectomy was less than that after lobectomy at 6 and 12 months, suggesting that segmentectomy may bring more benefits to patients [21]. In addition, we observed that in long-term follow-up, patients with stage IB MPA who received postoperative chemotherapy tended to have a better prognosis compared with those who did not receive chemotherapy, which is consistent with the findings of previous studies [22,23]. Therefore, we plan to predict the presence of MPA through non-invasive methods to guide the screening of patients suitable for adjuvant therapy. Therefore, we constructed a nomogram using univariate and multivariate logistic regression to predict the presence of MPA, aiming to guide the screening of patients suitable for adjuvant therapy.

Ultimately, our results identified smoking, CT-diameter ≥22.5 mm, PSN, SN and specific CT features – lobulation, spiculation, vacuoles, and VDT ≤310 days – as independent risk factors associated with the presence of MPA. These findings are consistent with previous literature suggesting that tumor size, lobulated margins, and lesion density are predictive markers of high-grade, poorly differentiated adenocarcinoma (HGP) on high-resolution CT (HRCT). Additionally, a study published in Radiology in 2020 [24] demonstrated that tumors with solid or micropapillary predominant histology had the shortest VDT, with a median of 229 days – closely aligning with the median VDT observed in MPA cases in our study. Given that VDT is a key imaging biomarker for distinguishing aggressive tumors from indolent ones, and is significantly associated with DFS in patients undergoing surgical resection [24], we incorporated VDT into our predictive model for MPA. Compared with conventional imaging features used in HGP prediction, the inclusion of VDT provides additional value in identifying highly aggressive MPA components. Finally, regarding imaging characteristics, this study focused on features that can be readily obtained through manual interpretation of CT scans to enable non-invasive prediction of MPA. CT diameter ≥22.5 mm, PSN, SN, lobulation, spiculation, vacuoles, and VDT ≤310 days were identified as independent predictors of MPA. The final logistic regression model incorporating these features achieved an AUC of 0.923, indicating excellent discriminatory performance. To enhance the clinical applicability and ease of use, we developed a simplified nomogram by assigning equal weights to the identified risk factors. To validate the calibration of the model, we used bootstrap for internal validation. As can be seen from Figure 3(B), the bias-corrected curve is very close to the ideal curve, indicating that the model has good calibration. The apparent curve also shows a relatively consistent trend with the ideal curve, suggesting that the model’s predicted probabilities are well-aligned with the observed MPA rates.

This study has several limitations. Although the proposed nomogram effectively stratified patients with lung adenocarcinoma into high- and low-risk groups for the presence of MPA, its ability to guide treatment decision-making was not fully demonstrated in the current analysis. Specifically, no significant prognostic differences were observed between high- and low-risk groups receiving different treatment modalities. This finding may be partly attributable to the substantial imbalance in treatment distribution (lobectomy vs. sublobar resection, approximately 9:1; adjuvant chemotherapy vs. no chemotherapy, approximately 1:5), as well as the relatively limited sample size, which precluded further stratified analyses across different pathological stages. Therefore, the potential role of nomogram-based risk stratification in informing individualized treatment strategies warrants further investigation in larger, multicenter cohorts, which are currently underway.

Patients with MPA have a significantly poorer prognosis compared to those without MPA. The MPA nomogram developed in this study enables more accurate risk stratification and offers a practical tool to support pathological evaluation and guide optimal treatment strategies in early-stage lung adenocarcinoma.
